title: What Is Software?
summary: Programs, files and running code - the words behind the magic.
objective: Explain what a program is, where software lives on your machine, and use the words file, folder, app and source code correctly when talking to your AI agent.

vocabulary.meaning: A list of instructions a computer follows in order.
The text version of a program that humans read and edit.
A named container for data on your computer - code, text, images are all files.
A container that groups related files together.
A program made for people to use - a notes app, a game, a website.

concepts.name: Code is text, software is action
concepts.explanation: Source code is plain text until something runs it. Your AI agent edits text files; the computer turns them into behavior. When people say 'run the app', they mean 'execute these instructions'.

concepts.name: Everything is a file
concepts.explanation: Your app's code, its settings, its images and even the record of what your agent did - all files in folders. If you can organize files, you can organize software.

explanations.title: Instructions, not intelligence
explanations.body: A program does exactly what its instructions say - nothing more. This is also true of your AI agent's output: it writes instructions for computers. Reading those instructions (the code) is how you stay the director.

explanations.title: Where software lives
explanations.body: Every app starts as a project folder somewhere on your disk. The folder holds the code files, settings files and assets. Knowing 'it is all just a folder' removes most of the fear.

examples.title: A calculator button
examples.description: When you tap '=' in a calculator app, a few lines of code take the numbers on screen, add them, and put the result back. That whole feature can be under ten lines of text.

examples.title: This curriculum site
examples.description: The page you are reading is files: layout files, style files and data files. A build step turned them into the site. Nothing more mysterious than that.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the AI agent 'understands' your goal the way a person would.
commonMistakes.fix: State the goal, the inputs and what 'done' looks like. The agent fills gaps by guessing - guesses you have to review.

commonMistakes.mistake: Never looking at the files the agent creates.
commonMistakes.fix: Open each new file once and ask the agent for a one-line summary. You are not learning to write code yet - you are learning to recognize it.

agentGuidance: When your agent scaffolds anything, follow up with: 'List every file you created and describe each in one sentence.' Make this a reflex from day one.

project.title: Vocabulary Notebook
project.brief: Have your agent build a single-page notebook that lists every term you learn in this curriculum - term on the left, meaning on the right. You will extend it as you learn.
requirements: One HTML file that opens directly in a browser by double-clicking it
Shows at least five terms with their meanings in a readable list or table
You can add a new term by asking the agent (and later, by copying the pattern yourself)
project.agentContext: Build a single self-contained HTML file called notebook.html with inline CSS. It must render a titled list of term-meaning pairs stored in one obvious place in the file so a beginner can find and copy the pattern. No JavaScript frameworks, no build step, no external dependencies.

functional: notebook.html opens in a browser with a double-click, no server needed
At least five term-meaning pairs are visible
Each pair renders as term plus meaning without overlap or broken layout
architecture: One self-contained file; terms defined in one clearly marked place
No external libraries or network requests
testing: Opened in a browser and visually confirmed all five entries render

verificationPrompt: Review my Vocabulary Notebook project. I asked my coding agent to build a single self-contained HTML file listing at least five term-meaning pairs. Check my actual file against this checklist and answer PASS or FAIL for each item with one line of evidence from the file itself: (1) opens standalone with no server or dependencies, (2) five or more term-meaning pairs present, (3) terms defined in one clearly marked place, (4) no external libraries or network requests. Then tell me: which assumption in my instructions most likely caused any FAIL, and the smallest fix.
reviewQuestions: In your own words: what is the difference between source code and a running program?
Your agent created four files. What question do you ask before trusting any of them?
Why is 'it is all just files in a folder' a useful thing to know?
capabilities: Use the words program, source code, file, folder and application accurately
Ask an agent to explain every file it creates
Open and inspect an HTML file without fear

title: Terminal Basics
summary: The text window where you and your agent actually drive the computer.
objective: Run basic terminal commands, understand what a working directory is, and read command output instead of fearing it.

vocabulary.meaning: A window where you type text commands instead of clicking buttons.
The program inside the terminal that reads and executes your commands.
A word plus optional arguments that tells the computer to do something specific.
The address of a file or folder, like documents/projects/my-app.
The folder your terminal is currently 'inside' - commands happen here.

concepts.name: Commands are just programs
concepts.explanation: Every command you type launches a small program. dir or ls lists folder contents; cd changes your working directory. There is no second hidden computer - the terminal is a direct line to the same files you see in Explorer or Finder.

concepts.name: Location changes meaning
concepts.explanation: The same command behaves differently depending on your working directory. Running a project's dev server from the wrong folder is the number-one beginner error.

explanations.title: Reading output top to bottom
explanations.body: Terminal output is a conversation. Errors usually appear last and often name the exact problem ('file not found', 'command not recognized'). Train yourself to read the last lines first - both for your own commands and for your agent's output.

explanations.title: Why agents live here too
explanations.body: AI coding agents run inside your terminal because that is where programs are started, tested and inspected. When your agent says it 'ran the tests', it typed commands into this same interface.

examples.title: Looking around
examples.description: pwd (or cd with no arguments on Windows) shows where you are; ls (dir on Windows) lists what is here; cd my-project moves you into a folder.

examples.title: The classic mistake
examples.description: Typing npm install in your home folder instead of the project folder creates junk files thousands of miles from where they belong. Always check your location first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running commands in the wrong folder.
commonMistakes.fix: Print your location (pwd or cd) before doing anything that changes files.

commonMistakes.mistake: Closing the terminal the moment red text appears.
commonMistakes.fix: Red text is information, not explosion. Copy the last lines and paste them to your agent - it diagnoses from exactly this evidence.

agentGuidance: Paste errors verbatim to your agent - never paraphrase them. The exact wording of an error is the diagnostic clue. Ask: 'Explain this error in one sentence, then give me the exact command to fix it.'

project.title: Command Journal
project.brief: Spend twenty minutes deliberately driving the terminal: move between folders, look inside them, create a file - then save a journal of what you ran and what happened.
requirements: Navigate to at least three different folders using cd
Create a folder and a text file from the terminal
Save a journal.txt containing at least ten commands you ran with a one-line note about what each did
project.agentContext: Do not build software for this project. Instead act as a terminal coach: suggest ten progressively interesting beginner-safe commands one at a time (navigation, listing, file creation, reading a file), wait for my paste-back of the result, and confirm or correct my understanding before the next one.

functional: journal.txt exists and contains at least ten commands with notes
At least one folder and one file were created from the terminal during the session
testing: Re-ran two commands from the journal and got the expected results

verificationPrompt: Act as a reviewer for my Command Journal exercise. I saved journal.txt with ten or more terminal commands and notes. Read the journal and check: (1) are all ten commands syntactically valid for my operating system, (2) do the notes match what each command actually does, (3) are any of them risky if re-run (deletion, overwriting)? Answer PASS or FAIL per point with evidence from the file, then name the one command whose purpose I most likely misunderstood.
reviewQuestions: What is your working directory right now, and how do you find out?
Your agent says 'tests failed' and prints red text. What do you do first?
Why does the same command behave differently in two folders?
capabilities: Navigate folders and run basic commands confidently
Read the last lines of terminal output first
Paste exact errors to an agent for diagnosis

title: Projects, Files and Structure
summary: What a project folder is, why structure matters, and the files every project has.
objective: Recognize the standard files in any modern project folder and explain what each one is for, so agent-created structures stop looking random.

vocabulary.meaning: One folder holding everything an application needs - code, settings and description files.
A file that stores settings so tools know how to treat the project.
Someone else's pre-built code package your project uses instead of rewriting it.
The front-door document explaining what a project is and how to run it.
The file where a program starts executing.

concepts.name: Conventions carry meaning
concepts.explanation: Tools expect certain names: package.json tells JavaScript tools what your project needs, README.md introduces it to humans. Following conventions lets every tool - including agents - orient instantly.

concepts.name: Dependencies are borrowed strength
concepts.explanation: Modern apps are mostly assembled from packages other people published. A manifest file lists what you borrow; a lockfile pins exact versions. More dependencies mean more power and more surface area to maintain.

explanations.title: Reading a project folder like a map
explanations.body: Top level: manifest files (what this project is and needs), README (how to use it), source folders (where code lives), config files (how tools should behave). When your agent generates a new project, walk this map out loud with it once.

explanations.title: Structure is communication
explanations.body: Folders group things that change together: UI code near UI code, settings near settings. Good structure makes the next change easy to find; bad structure makes even the agent guess.

examples.title: Two files every repo has
examples.description: README.md answers 'what is this and how do I run it'; the manifest (like package.json) answers 'what does it depend on'. Open both first in any unfamiliar project.

examples.title: node_modules is rented furniture
examples.description: Downloaded dependencies land in a folder you never hand-edit and never need to back up - it can be rebuilt from the manifest anytime.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the agent scatter files randomly across the project.
commonMistakes.fix: Insist on one conventional layout: 'Follow standard Next.js structure and explain the role of each top-level file.'

commonMistakes.mistake: Hand-editing lockfiles or downloaded dependency folders.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the manifest through the package manager command; regenerate the rest.

agentGuidance: After any scaffold, ask: 'Show me the project tree and label each top-level entry: mine-to-edit, tool-generated-but-readable, or never-touch.' Keep this map in your head for every future project.

project.title: Project Blueprint
project.brief: Create the skeleton of a real web project - not a working app yet, just the honest bones: README, manifest-style metadata and an organized folder plan you generate with your agent.
requirements: A project folder named blueprint with a README.md describing purpose and how someone would run it
A valid package.json with name, version, description and license fields
src/ and public/ folders present with a one-line placeholder file in each explaining its future role
project.agentContext: Scaffold a minimal static web project folder called blueprint: package.json with sensible metadata, README.md written in plain language for a newcomer, src/ and public/ directories each containing a PLACEHOLDER.md one-liner about the folder's purpose. Use standard conventions only; no installed dependencies, no build tooling.

functional: blueprint folder contains README.md, package.json, src/, public/
package.json parses as valid JSON with name, version, description and license
README explains the project's purpose and a hypothetical run step
architecture: Folder layout follows common conventions with no stray root files
testing: Ran a JSON validator against package.json and it passed

verificationPrompt: Review my Project Blueprint folder. Check against this Definition of Done and answer PASS or FAIL per item using evidence from the actual files: (1) contains exactly README.md, package.json, src/ and public/ with nothing stray at the root, (2) package.json is valid JSON with name, version, description, license, (3) README states purpose plus a plausible run instruction, (4) each placeholder file describes its folder's role in one line. Then tell me which convention a professional reviewer would say I got most wrong, if any.
reviewQuestions: Which two files do you open first in an unfamiliar project, and why?
What is the difference between a manifest and a lockfile?
Why should you never hand-edit downloaded dependency folders?
capabilities: Read any project folder's structure and explain its parts
Instruct an agent to follow conventions instead of inventing layouts
Explain what dependencies are and where they live

title: Working With AI Coding Agents
summary: What agents can do, how they fail, and how to direct them instead of hoping.
objective: Direct an AI coding agent with structured instructions, understand context windows and failure modes, and build the review habit that keeps you in charge.

vocabulary.meaning: The instruction text you give an AI model or agent.
Everything the agent can currently see - your messages, files, prior replies.
The finite amount of context an agent can hold at once.
An agent's action on the world: reading a file, editing code, running a command.
When an AI states something false with complete confidence.

concepts.name: Specify, do not wish
concepts.explanation: 'Make it better' forces the agent to guess what better means. Goal, constraints and definition of done turn wishes into work orders. Vague input produces confident nonsense; specific input produces reviewable output.

concepts.name: Context is finite and precious
concepts.explanation: Agents forget what falls out of their context window. Long sessions drift. Re-stating key facts, pointing at specific files, and starting fresh sessions per task are professional habits, not quirks.

explanations.title: The delegation loop
explanations.body: Directing an agent is a loop: state the task, let it work, inspect the diff, test the result, correct with specifics. The loop never skips inspection - that is what separates directing from gambling.

explanations.title: Failure modes you will meet
explanations.body: Hallucinated APIs (functions that do not exist), silent scope creep (changing files you did not ask about), and overconfident claims ('all tests pass' when none ran). Each has the same antidote: verify against reality, not against the agent's confidence.

examples.title: Weak prompt vs strong prompt
examples.description: 'Add login to my app' versus 'Add email-and-password login: form validates non-empty, wrong credentials show a generic error, successful login redirects to /home. Do not touch other pages.' Same agent, completely different outcomes.

examples.title: Asking for the diff
examples.description: 'Show me exactly which files you changed and summarize each change in one line' turns a black box into a reviewable change set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accepting large changes without reading them.
commonMistakes.fix: Require a per-file summary for anything over a couple of files, and skim each file once before approving.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pasting passwords, keys or personal data into prompts.
commonMistakes.fix: Treat prompt text as semi-public. Reference secrets indirectly ('read from .env.local') and never paste their values.

agentGuidance: Adopt a standing instruction template for real tasks: goal, constraints, definition of done, and 'summarize changed files when finished'. Save it somewhere and reuse it every time.

project.title: The Briefing Document
project.brief: Write a one-page spec for a small app idea of yours - written so well that an agent (or a person) could build it without asking you a single clarifying question.
requirements: States the app's purpose in two sentences
Lists concrete features with acceptance criteria for each (what proves it works)
Lists explicit non-goals (what it should NOT include)
Names its constraints: single user, no payment, no accounts
project.agentContext: Do not write any code. Act as a demanding technical editor for my spec document: challenge every vague phrase, mark each feature missing an acceptance criterion, and return the improved outline as a list of gaps - not a rewrite. I will fix the gaps myself.

functional: Document covers purpose, features with acceptance criteria, non-goals and constraints
Every feature has at least one testable acceptance criterion
A fresh reading requires zero assumed knowledge
architecture: One page, four clear sections in the listed order
security: Contains no real secrets, emails or personal data in examples
testing: Asked the agent to list gaps in the doc and resolved every gap it raised

verificationPrompt: You are auditing my Briefing Document for build-readiness. Read it as if you were the developer receiving it. Answer PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) purpose understandable in two sentences, (2) every feature has a testable acceptance criterion, (3) non-goals explicitly fence the scope, (4) constraints section exists with no contradictions elsewhere in the doc. Then list any question you would still need to ask me before building from it - if you have none, say so explicitly.
reviewQuestions: Rewrite 'make it look nicer' as a strong prompt for your agent.
Name two failure modes of AI agents and the antidote for each.
Why is context described as 'finite and precious'?
capabilities: Write structured briefs that remove agent guesswork
Recognize hallucinations, scope creep and unverified claims
Keep secrets out of conversations with agents

title: Git Through Your Agent
summary: Repositories, commits and branches - your project's undo button and story book.
objective: Understand what git records, direct your agent to commit work in meaningful steps, and recover from mistakes using history instead of panic.

vocabulary.meaning: A project folder whose full history of changes git remembers.
A saved snapshot of your project at one moment, with a message describing why.
A parallel line of development you can experiment on safely.
Combining one branch's changes into another.
A copy of the repository hosted elsewhere, like GitHub.

concepts.name: History is a safety net
concepts.explanation: Every commit is a restore point. Break something? Go back to the last good commit. Small frequent commits shrink the blast radius of every mistake - including your agent's mistakes.

concepts.name: Commit messages are the story
concepts.explanation: Six months from now, the log is the only witness to why the code looks this way. 'Fix stuff' tells nothing; 'validate email format on signup' tells the next reader exactly what happened.

explanations.title: The three questions after any change
explanations.body: git status shows what changed, git diff (via your agent) shows how it changed, git log shows the story so far. Direct your agent to show you all three whenever you resume work.

explanations.title: Branches make experiments cheap
explanations.body: Trying a risky change? Branch first. If it fails, delete the branch - main stays clean. Agents handle the mechanics; you decide when an experiment deserves its own branch.

examples.title: Undo via history
examples.description: Agent broke the homepage? Restore the last good commit's files - no archaeology required. This single ability changes how boldly you can experiment.

examples.title: Reading a good log
examples.description: 'add expense delete button', 'fix total ignoring currency', 'deploy v1' - six months later this log still explains the app's evolution line by line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing rarely, in giant blobs.
commonMistakes.fix: One logical change per commit. Tell your agent: 'Commit now' at natural checkpoints instead of end-of-day dumps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing secrets or .env files.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep a .gitignore from day one and ask the agent to verify staged files before every commit.

agentGuidance: Standardize commit messages with your agent up front: imperative mood, one line, why-focused. Example standing rule: 'Every commit message: verb first, max 72 characters, describe the why when it is not obvious.'

project.title: Time Machine
project.brief: Build a tiny text project entirely through git: create a repo with your agent and evolve a single ideas.txt across at least five meaningful commits, including one experiment on a branch that you deliberately discard.
requirements: Repository initialized with at least five commits total
Each commit message follows the agreed convention (verb-first, descriptive)
One branch named experiment with a change that gets deleted without merging
Final git log tells a readable story of the file's evolution
project.agentContext: Initialize a git repository in a new folder. Coach me through evolving ideas.txt across five commits I dictate, enforcing my commit-message convention before each commit. Then create an experiment branch, make one change there, and teach me to abandon the branch cleanly. Show me git log and git status at the end and explain both outputs.

functional: Repository exists with ideas.txt evolved across at least five commits
experiment branch was created, changed and discarded without merging
git log output shows verb-first messages telling a coherent story
security: No secrets or personal files committed; .gitignore excludes junk
testing: Verified the discarded branch left no trace on the default branch's content

verificationPrompt: Audit my Time Machine repository as a git reviewer. Run git log yourself if you can. Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) at least five commits touching ideas.txt, (2) every message verb-first and descriptive, (3) an experiment branch existed and its changes are absent from the final default branch, (4) no committed secrets or junk files. Then show me the single most confusing commit message and rewrite it per my convention.
reviewQuestions: Your agent just wrecked a working file. What is your recovery move?
What belongs in a commit message that 'fixed bug' leaves out?
Why create a branch before a risky experiment?
capabilities: Direct an agent to commit in meaningful, well-described steps
Recover any mistake from history instead of redoing work
Keep secrets out of repository history

title: Anatomy of a Web App
summary: Frontend, backend, database - the map you need before building anything.
objective: Explain how a web app's pieces fit together - browser, server, database - and trace what happens when a user clicks a button, using the words request, response and JSON precisely.

vocabulary.meaning: The part of an app that runs in the user's browser - what they see and click.
The part running on a server - logic, secrets, and the door to the database.
Software that remembers data permanently, organized for fast retrieval.
The message a browser sends a server asking for data or an action.
The server's reply - data, or an error code.
The text format almost all APIs use to exchange structured data.

concepts.name: The three-layer map
concepts.explanation: Browser (frontend) talks to a server (backend), which talks to a database. Data flows as requests and responses. Every app you use - from a blog to a bank - fits this map; complexity hides in the details, not in extra layers.

concepts.name: The request-response cycle
concepts.explanation: Click a button and the browser may send a request: 'create this expense'. The backend validates it, touches the database, and responds: success plus the saved record, or an error code. Tracing this cycle is debugging skill number one.

explanations.title: Why the split exists
explanations.body: The frontend must be fast and pretty; the backend must be trustworthy and secret-keeping; the database must remember. Different jobs, different layers. When your agent proposes putting a secret in frontend code, this map tells you why that is wrong.

explanations.title: Status codes are the truth serum
explanations.body: 200 means ok, 404 means nothing there, 500 means the server broke. Agents and browsers both lie less than status codes. Checking the status code is how you verify 'it works' claims.

examples.title: Loading a page
examples.description: Browser asks the server for the page; server returns HTML; browser requests the styles and scripts referenced; each comes back with a status code. That cascade happens in under a second.

examples.title: Saving a todo
examples.description: Submit sends a POST request carrying JSON; backend saves to database; response confirms. Refresh the page - the todo survives because it lives in the database now, not in your browser tab.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the browser 'contains' the data.
commonMistakes.fix: Browser tabs hold copies. Truth lives behind responses. If data matters, it belongs in a database.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting 'it works' without checking the network layer.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask your agent to show the actual request and response - URL, status code, body - for any feature that talks to a server.

agentGuidance: New superpower: when a feature misbehaves, ask your agent to 'trace this interaction end to end - which request fires, what status came back, what did the server log?' You are asking for the cycle, not vibes.

project.title: Anatomy Lab
project.brief: With your agent, build a tiny local web page that demonstrates its own existence: it displays its request-response story live - a button triggers a fetch to a free no-key API and shows the raw request URL, the returned status code and a snippet of the JSON response.
requirements: Single page runs locally with a simple start command
One button performs a real HTTP request to https://api.open-meteo.com (no key needed)
Page displays: the requested URL, the returned status code, and formatted sample JSON from the response
A short section on the page explains the three-layer map in your own words
project.agentContext: Build a minimal local web app: one page, one button. On click, fetch current weather for a hardcoded city from api.open-meteo.com (free, keyless). Display the request URL, HTTP status code and a formatted excerpt of the JSON response in monospace text. Include a short human-written section explaining the frontend-backend-database map. Keep styling minimal; prioritize clarity over beauty.

functional: App starts locally with one command and loads in a browser
Button click performs a real network call to the weather API
URL, status code and JSON excerpt all visibly update after the click
Three-layer explanation section present in the author's own words
architecture: Single page, one obvious fetch call, no framework overhead
security: No secrets in code - the chosen API requires none
testing: Clicked the button with the network disconnected and observed a handled failure state instead of a silent break

verificationPrompt: Review my Anatomy Lab app as a senior engineer. Verify with evidence, PASS or FAIL each: (1) one-command local start, (2) button triggers a genuine fetch to api.open-meteo.com with no API key involved, (3) request URL, status code and JSON excerpt render after click, (4) offline click produces a visible handled error rather than silence, (5) no secrets anywhere in the code. Then trace one full button-click interaction end to end - naming the request, the response status, and where each piece of displayed data came from.
reviewQuestions: Trace what happens from button press to screen update in your Anatomy Lab.
Where should a password check happen - frontend or backend - and why?
What does a 404 status code tell you that a blank screen does not?
capabilities: Map any app onto the frontend-backend-database picture
Trace a click through request and response
Verify behavior with status codes instead of trusting appearances

title: Components and User Interfaces
summary: Building screens from reusable pieces - the Lego bricks of every modern app.
objective: Think in components - reusable UI pieces with inputs (props) and internal memory (state) - and direct an agent to compose interfaces instead of hand-crafting one-off screens.

vocabulary.meaning: A self-contained, reusable piece of interface - a button, a card, a navbar.
Data passed INTO a component to configure it, like arguments to a function.
Data a component remembers internally that can change over time.
The act of turning component data into what you see on screen.
A toolkit (React, Vue, etc.) that standardizes how components are written and updated.

concepts.name: UI is a function of data
concepts.explanation: Modern frameworks redraw the screen automatically when state changes. You describe what the screen should look like for any given data; the machinery handles updating the pixels. Stop thinking in steps - think in states.

concepts.name: Composition beats duplication
concepts.explanation: One ExpenseCard component rendered forty times beats forty copy-pasted blocks. Change the component once, all forty update. Duplication is where UI bugs breed.

explanations.title: Spotting components everywhere
explanations.body: Open any app: the video card, the sidebar item, the avatar bubble - each is likely ONE component fed DIFFERENT props. Training your eye to see the repeated unit is the core frontend skill.

explanations.title: Props down, events up
explanations.body: Data flows into components via props; components report user actions upward via events/callbacks. When your diagram of who-knows-what gets tangled, that is the smell prompting you to restructure state.

examples.title: One card, many products
examples.description: A shop page is one ProductCard component receiving name, price and image as props, rendered in a list. The 'page' is barely code at all - it is data mapped through one good component.

examples.title: State you can point at
examples.description: A counter has one piece of state (the count) and two events (+/-). Being able to enumerate an app's states like this is how you review an agent's UI work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accepting copy-pasted near-identical UI blocks from the agent.
commonMistakes.fix: Rule for your agent: 'If markup repeats twice with different data, extract a component taking props.'

commonMistakes.mistake: Storing the same fact in five places.
commonMistakes.fix: One owner per piece of state; everyone else receives props. Ask the agent to name the single owner of each fact.

agentGuidance: Before letting the agent build UI, make it list the components it plans, the props each takes, and which component owns each piece of state. Approve the PLAN, then let it code. Reviewing a component list takes a minute; reviewing tangled UI takes an hour.

project.title: Card Gallery
project.brief: Direct your agent to build a gallery of cards from a data array - then prove composition works by changing the DATA ONLY and watching the UI update correctly.
requirements: One Card component rendering title, description and a tag
Gallery renders at least six cards driven purely from a single data array
Editing one array entry (no other file touched) updates exactly that card
Empty array produces a friendly empty-state message, not a blank screen
project.agentContext: Build a small gallery app: a single Card component (title, description, tag) rendered repeatedly from one data array of at least six entries, plus a graceful empty state. First show me the planned component tree and state ownership for approval; implement only after I approve. No styling frameworks - clean minimal CSS is fine.

functional: All six cards render from the data array
Changing one array entry updates exactly that card after reload/re-render
Emptying the array shows a designed empty state
architecture: Exactly one Card component; zero duplicated card markup
Component list and state ownership documented in the README
testing: Performed the data-only edit test and confirmed isolated updates
Rendered the empty-array case intentionally

verificationPrompt: Review my Card Gallery. Inspect the code and verify PASS or FAIL with file-level evidence: (1) a single Card component exists and no card markup is duplicated, (2) cards render exclusively from one data array - no hardcoded cards in markup, (3) an empty array yields the designed empty state, (4) README documents the component list and which piece owns each state. Then try renaming a field in the data array yourself and tell me every place that breaks - that reveals hidden couplings.
reviewQuestions: Pick any app on your phone: name three components inside it.
What is the difference between a prop and state, in one sentence each?
Why did we demand a component plan BEFORE letting the agent write UI?
capabilities: See interfaces as compositions of reusable components
Demand component plans before approving agent UI work
Test UI changes by editing data, not markup

title: Forms and Input Validation
summary: Getting data from humans safely - and never trusting a single character of it.
objective: Direct an agent to build forms that collect input, validate it against explicit rules, show helpful errors, and treat every input as untrusted - your first real security habit.

vocabulary.meaning: The UI pattern for collecting input: fields, labels, a submit action.
Checking submitted values against rules before accepting them.
Something the user does that code reacts to - typing, submitting, clicking.
The designed way your UI behaves when input breaks the rules.
Cleaning or rejecting input that could be dangerous, not just wrong.

concepts.name: Users will type anything
concepts.explanation: Empty submissions, 500-character names, emails without @, scripts pasted into fields. Assume every field will receive the worst possible value and design rules for it upfront.

concepts.name: Validation is a security habit
concepts.explanation: Checking input is your first line of defense, long before authentication enters the picture. The discipline you build here - explicit rules, reject early, explain failures - scales directly to server-side security later.

explanations.title: Rules as a contract
explanations.body: Write validation rules as a visible list: username 3-20 characters, letters and numbers only; email matches a basic pattern; password at least 8 characters. The list IS the specification - your agent codes the list, your tests check the list, your reviewers audit the list.

explanations.title: Errors help, they do not scold
explanations.body: 'Invalid input' helps nobody. 'Password must be at least 8 characters' lets the user succeed. Every error message should state the rule that was broken.

examples.title: The three-layer check
examples.description: Required field empty -> block submit, highlight the field. Email malformed -> message under the field. All valid -> success state. Walking the happy path AND each failure path is how you verify a form.

examples.title: Dangerous input example
examples.description: A comment box that renders whatever users type can execute scripts attackers paste into it. Rejecting or escaping such input is sanitizing - a preview of XSS, which you will meet properly in Level 2.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only testing the happy path.
commonMistakes.fix: Test every rule with a violating input, plus empty-everything submit. Your DoD should list them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Vague error messages like 'Error!' or nothing at all.
commonMistakes.fix: Every broken rule maps to one specific, human message naming the rule.

agentGuidance: Give your agent the rules table FIRST, then ask it to enumerate the failure cases it will implement BEFORE coding. You review the case list - that is faster than reviewing code hunting for missed cases.

project.title: Signup Form With Rules

Submitting invalid input blocks and shows a specific message under each offending field
Valid submission shows a designed success state (no real accounts being created)

Show a specific error message beneath each failing field on submit; block submission while any rule fails; show a success panel when all pass. Before coding, print the list of failure cases you will cover so I can approve it.

functional: All three fields validate against the stated rules
Invalid submits are blocked with per-field, rule-specific messages
Valid input reaches the success state
Empty-form submit shows all three errors simultaneously
architecture: Rules exist in one obvious place matching the documented table
security: No input value is ever inserted into the page as raw HTML
Browser console stays clean of unhandled errors during abuse attempts
testing: Demoed every failure path: empty, bad email, short password, bad username
Demoed the success path end to end

verificationPrompt: Security-review my Signup Form. Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) all three rules implemented exactly as specified, (2) each failing field shows ITS OWN rule-naming message, (3) invalid submits are fully blocked, (4) no user input is rendered as raw HTML anywhere, (5) success state reachable only with all rules passing. Then attack the form yourself: try five abusive inputs (script tags, 10000-char strings, weird unicode) and report how the form behaved on each.
reviewQuestions: Recite your form's rules table from memory.
Why is 'invalid input' a bad error message?
How does form validation preview real security thinking?

Verify forms by walking failure paths, not just the happy path
Apply never-trust-input as a standing security habit

title: APIs and JSON
summary: How apps talk to each other - endpoints, requests, responses and the shape of data.
objective: Consume a real API through your agent: read endpoint documentation, handle success and failure responses, and parse JSON confidently.

vocabulary.meaning: Application Programming Interface - a defined way for programs to request services from each other.
One specific URL an API exposes, like /weather or /users/42.
The common web style where URLs name resources and HTTP methods name actions.
The number in every response classifying the outcome: 200 ok, 404 missing, 500 broken.
A cap on how many calls you may make in a time window.

concepts.name: APIs are contracts
concepts.explanation: Documentation promises: send this, receive that. Your code trusts the contract; the provider may version or change it. Reading docs before coding - and having your agent quote the relevant doc lines - prevents fantasy integrations.

concepts.name: Failure is a first-class case
concepts.explanation: Networks drop, servers hiccup, limits trip. Code that only handles the happy path is a bug factory. Every API call deserves a designed failure state: retry hint, cached data, or honest error message.

explanations.title: Reading a JSON response
explanations.body: JSON nests objects {} and arrays []. Top to bottom: what type is the root, where is the array, what fields does each element carry, which fields hold nested objects. Print the raw JSON once and walk it before writing display code.

explanations.title: Keys, secrets and the frontend
explanations.body: Some APIs require keys proving who is calling. A key in frontend code is public the moment you ship - anyone can read it. Keyless APIs (like Open-Meteo) are perfect for learning; keyed ones belong behind a backend, which you will build in Level 2.

examples.title: One endpoint, two futures
examples.description: GET api.example.com/users/7 returns 200 with a JSON user - or 404 with an error object. Your code branches on status first, then parses. Status-first parsing is the professional habit.

examples.title: Rate limits in the wild
examples.description: Free tiers often allow ~60 calls per hour. Polling every second burns through it and returns 429 Too Many Requests. Respect limits or cache aggressively.

commonMistakes.mistake: Parsing before checking the status code.
commonMistakes.fix: Branch on status: 2xx parse onward, else handle the failure path explicitly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hardcoding API keys into frontend code.
commonMistakes.fix: Prefer keyless APIs while frontend-only; move keyed calls behind a backend in Level 2.

agentGuidance: Before any integration, require your agent to produce a three-line integration note: endpoint(s) used, auth requirements, rate limit. If it cannot cite the docs, it has not read them - send it back to read.

project.title: Live Data Widget
project.brief: Extend your Anatomy Lab skills into a purposeful widget: pick any keyless public API and build a focused display of one slice of its data, with designed loading, error and empty states.
requirements: Uses a public API requiring NO key (cite it in the README)
Displays a focused slice of live data (not a raw JSON dump)
Three designed states: loading, failure with retry affordance, success
README documents the endpoint(s), their documented limits and the data slice shown
project.agentContext: Help me choose a keyless public API suited to a small widget (suggest three options with trade-offs). After I pick one, build a minimal widget showing one focused data slice with explicit loading, error (with retry) and success states. Quote the API documentation lines for endpoints and rate limits into the README. No frameworks unless I approve.

functional: Widget renders live data from the chosen API on load
Loading state appears during the request
Killing the network shows the failure state with a working retry
Displayed data matches a manual curl/browser check of the same endpoint
architecture: Status checked before parsing; each state explicitly handled
security: Chosen API requires no key; zero secrets in the repo
testing: Triggered all three states manually and screenshot/verified each
Compared displayed values against the raw endpoint response once

verificationPrompt: Review my Live Data Widget. Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) uses only keyless endpoints and the README cites the API docs, (2) HTTP status is checked before parsing, (3) loading, failure-with-retry and success states are all implemented and reachable, (4) displayed values correspond to the real API response schema, (5) no secrets in code or git history. Then hit the endpoint yourself and tell me whether my code would survive: a 10-second delay, a 500 response, and a schema change moving the data one level deeper.
reviewQuestions: What does your widget do differently when the status is 500 versus 404?
Why is a frontend API key effectively public?
Walk through your JSON's shape: root type, array location, element fields.
capabilities: Integrate real APIs by reading contracts, not guessing
Design all response states, not just success
Keep keys out of frontend code by choosing the right architecture

title: Databases and CRUD
summary: Making data outlive the browser - tables, rows and the four verbs of every app.
objective: Understand persistent storage, direct an agent to build a Create-Read-Update-Delete application, and verify data truly survives restarts.

vocabulary.meaning: Software that stores data durably and retrieves it efficiently.
A collection of same-shaped records - like a spreadsheet with enforced columns.
One entry in a table - one expense, one user.
Create, Read, Update, Delete - the four operations nearly every app performs on data.
The declared shape of your data: which fields exist and their types.
A request for data meeting certain conditions.

concepts.name: Persistence changes everything
concepts.explanation: Until now, closing the tab erased your app's memory. A database writes data to disk: restart, reboot, revisit tomorrow - it is still there. Persistence is the line between toys and tools.

concepts.name: CRUD is the grammar of apps
concepts.explanation: Notes apps: create notes, read them, edit, delete. Shops: products and orders. Feeds: posts. Once you see CRUD, you see that most apps differ in domain, not mechanics - which is why agents build them so well WHEN you specify the schema.

explanations.title: Schema first, always
explanations.body: Decide the shape before the screens: an expense has amount (number), category (text), date (date), note (optional text). Four fields - that decision drives storage, forms, display and validation. Schema-first keeps the agent honest and your reviews fast.

explanations.title: Where the database lives at Level 1
explanations.body: Local options (SQLite file, browser storage backed by a tiny library) are fine now. The multi-user questions - who can touch whose rows - arrive with Level 2's servers. Do not solve sharing problems before having the sharing problem.

examples.title: The restart test
examples.description: Create an expense, close everything, reopen. Still there? Persistence verified. This thirty-second ritual is your database's most important test.

examples.title: Update versus create confusion
examples.description: Editing an existing expense must NOT insert a duplicate row. If your app grows a second identical entry after an edit, the update path is really creating - a classic agent bug worth hunting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping the schema conversation and letting the agent improvise fields.
commonMistakes.fix: Declare the schema explicitly in your brief; make the agent echo it back before coding.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting the UI as proof of saving.
commonMistakes.fix: Verify persistence by restarting, not by watching the list update on screen.

agentGuidance: Standing rule for CRUD projects: 'Echo the schema before implementing. After implementing, demonstrate each CRUD operation against the actual store and show me the evidence.' Screenshots of UI prove nothing; queries against data prove everything.

project.title: Expense Tracker v1
project.brief: The flagship Level 1 build: a single-user expense tracker with full CRUD on a real persistent store, schema declared by you, verified by restarts - not screenshots.

Full CRUD: add, view list sorted newest first, edit existing, delete with confirmation
Data persists across full app restarts
Total of all expenses visible and correct

Negative amounts and empty categories are rejected with specific messages

Delete requires confirmation
security: Input validated before touching the store
No raw user input interpolated into queries (ask the agent how it parameterizes - and understand the answer)
testing: Restart test passed twice

Total recalculates correctly after every operation type
production: Store file/location documented in README with backup hint (copy the file)

Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) schema matches amount/category/date/note exactly, (2) all CRUD operations demonstrably work against persistence (perform them yourself if you can), (3) editing never duplicates rows, (4) totals are computed from stored data, not tracked separately, (5) validation rejects negative amounts and empty categories, (6) store access is parameterized, not string-concatenated. What went wrong if editing creates a second identical row?

Build and verify full CRUD on persistent storage
Prove persistence with restarts and store-level checks

title: Shipping Your First App
summary: From localhost to a real URL anyone on earth can open.
objective: Deploy your Expense Tracker to public hosting, understand builds and environment configuration, and establish the ship-verify-rollback rhythm.

vocabulary.meaning: Making your app available on a public server instead of only your machine.
The process turning source code into optimized files ready to serve.
A service (Vercel, Netlify, etc.) that runs your deployed app.
Configuration supplied to the app from outside the code - URLs, flags, secrets.
Reverting a deployment to the previous working version.

concepts.name: localhost is not the internet
concepts.explanation: Your machine differs from a server: OS, paths, environment variables, network. Deployment surprises come from exactly these differences. The cure is deploying EARLY and OFTEN - every week, not at the end.

concepts.name: Builds freeze reality
concepts.explanation: A deployment serves the built snapshot, not your live editor. Changed code without a rebuild changes nothing on the public URL. Know which revision your URL serves - hosting dashboards show it.

explanations.title: Configuration lives outside code
explanations.body: Settings that differ between your laptop and production (API base URLs, feature flags) belong in environment variables, never hardcoded. The twelve-factor habit: code is constant, config varies by environment.

explanations.title: Ship, verify, roll back
explanations.body: Deployment is not done at 'Deploy Succeeded'. Open the live URL, perform the restart test against production, check the critical flows. Broken? Roll back to the previous deployment - platforms keep history precisely for this. Shipping is a rhythm, not an event.

examples.title: The classic deploy surprise
examples.description: Works locally, crashes live: cause is usually an unset environment variable or a path case-sensitivity difference. Read the platform's runtime logs - they name the exact error.

examples.title: Rollback in practice
examples.description: Bad deploy at 4pm; users see errors. Rollback to 3pm's deployment takes one click and restores service while you debug calmly. This is why platforms retain deployment history.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deploying once at the end of a project.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy in week one, then continuously. Small diffs between deployments make problems findable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Announcing the launch before verifying the live URL yourself.
commonMistakes.fix: Personal ritual: run your own Definition of Done against PRODUCTION before sharing any link.

agentGuidance: Have your agent prepare a pre-deploy checklist specific to your stack (env vars needed, build command, health check), then walk it with you on every deploy. Agents know platform quirks; make them write the checklist down.

project.title: Expense Tracker, Shipped

requirements: Live public URL serving the tracker (free tier hosting is fine)

One deliberate rollback performed and documented (deploy a broken marker, verify, roll back)
README updated: live URL, platform, env vars needed (even if none), how to run locally and deployed

architecture: Environment-specific values come from environment variables, not hardcoded strings
security: No secrets in the deployed bundle or the repository

testing: Full DoD executed against PRODUCTION, not localhost
Platform runtime logs checked once and understood
production: README documents live URL, platform, env vars, local-run and deploy steps
Rollback method known and rehearsed (not theoretical)

Your live site breaks after a deploy - what are your first three moves?

Keep configuration out of code

title: Servers and Backends
summary: Your code running on someone else's request - routes, handlers and honest status codes.
objective: Run a backend server locally, explain how routes map to handler functions, and expose a real JSON API that answers with correct status codes.

vocabulary.meaning: A long-running program that listens for requests and sends responses.
The pairing of an HTTP method and URL path with the function that handles it.
The function that runs when a request hits its route.
The numbered door on a machine where a server listens, like 3000.
The verb of a request - GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes.

concepts.name: A server is just your program, listening
concepts.explanation: Strip the mystique: a backend is code that starts, binds to a port, and loops forever answering requests. You have run programs since Level 0; this one happens to answer the phone.

concepts.name: Routes are a switchboard
concepts.explanation: GET /expenses goes to listExpenses(), POST /expenses goes to createExpenses(). Same URL, different methods, different jobs. When you can enumerate an API's route table from memory, you understand the app's surface area.

explanations.title: Status codes are your API's body language
explanations.body: 200 created-or-found, 400 you sent garbage, 401 you are not logged in, 403 you may not, 404 no such thing, 500 I broke. An API that returns 200 for everything - including failures - is lying to every client that trusts it.

explanations.title: Why backends hold the power
explanations.body: Frontend code ships to strangers; backend code stays home. Secrets, real validation and database access live server-side precisely because nobody can tamper with what they cannot touch.

examples.title: One handler, dissected
examples.description: POST /expenses receives JSON, validates amount is a positive number, asks the store layer to save, replies 201 with the saved record - or 400 naming exactly which field failed. Four steps, same skeleton as every handler you will ever review.

examples.title: curl is your UI
examples.description: curl http://localhost:3000/expenses exercises the API directly, bypassing any interface. Backend developers live in this mode because UIs hide what the API actually said.

commonMistakes.mistake: Verifying API behavior only through the app's screens.
commonMistakes.fix: Exercise endpoints directly with curl or an agent-run script; the screen is one consumer, not the contract.

commonMistakes.mistake: Returning 200 with an error message inside the body.
commonMistakes.fix: Match status to outcome. Clients branch on codes; make them truthful.

agentGuidance: Require your agent to print the full route table at startup and provide a sample curl for each route in the README. A route table you can read is a surface you can defend and test.

project.title: Expense API
project.brief: Rebuild the tracker's brain as a standalone HTTP API - no screens, pure endpoints - so every future module can build on a real, testable service.
requirements: Endpoints: GET /health, GET /expenses, POST /expenses, PUT /expenses/:id, DELETE /expenses/:id
POST/PUT validate amount positive number and category required; violations return 400 naming the field
Unknown routes return 404; DELETE on missing id returns 404

Invalid POST/PUT payloads return 400 naming each offending field
Missing resources return 404, not crashes or empty 200s
Restart test: created expense still present after server restart
architecture: Route handlers stay thin; storage logic lives in one store layer
Error responses share one consistent JSON shape
security: Server-side validation rejects malformed JSON and wrong types outright
Port and environment-specific values come from env vars, not hardcoded strings
testing: A scripted curl pass exercises happy path AND failure paths end to end
Every documented curl example was executed successfully once
production: Start command and full route table documented in README

Why does validation belong in the server even though the form already checks?

Test backends directly instead of through screens

title: Relational Data Modeling
summary: Tables that reference each other - foreign keys, joins and migrations that do not break things.
objective: Model multi-user data as related tables, enforce integrity with foreign keys, evolve schema safely through migrations, and prove relationships with join queries.

vocabulary.meaning: The unique id identifying each row in a table.
A column referencing another table's primary key, linking rows together.
A relation where one row owns many others - one user, many expenses.
A query combining rows from related tables.
A versioned, repeatable script that changes the database schema.
The guarantee that a foreign key always points at a real row.

concepts.name: Reference, never duplicate
concepts.explanation: When expenses belong to users, each expense stores user_id - not a copied username. One source of truth: change the username once, everywhere correct. Duplicated facts drift out of sync and lie eventually.

concepts.name: Migrations are version control for schema
concepts.explanation: Schema changes ship as ordered scripts that run the same way everywhere - your laptop, teammates, production. Hand-tweaking a live database outside migrations is how environments silently diverge.

explanations.title: From flat file to relations
explanations.body: Level 1 stored expenses anonymously because there were no users. Multi-user changes everything: WHOSE expense becomes part of the data itself. That single foreign key unlocks permissions, filtering, and every team feature you will ever build.

explanations.title: Integrity at the database level
explanations.body: App code can have bugs; constraints cannot be bypassed by a forgotten check. A foreign key constraint makes an orphan row physically impossible - the database itself refuses. Defense in depth starts with letting the storage layer carry some of the weight.

examples.title: The join that proves the model
examples.description: SELECT expenses.amount, users.name FROM expenses JOIN users ON expenses.user_id = users.id - one query, both tables, each expense displayed beside its owner's name. If your join works, your keys are right.

examples.title: Constraint refusing an orphan
examples.description: Inserting an expense whose user_id is 999 when no such user exists fails with a foreign key error. That refusal is a feature: corrupted relationships cannot enter the database even through buggy code.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting the application to keep references valid without DB constraints.
commonMistakes.fix: Declare foreign key constraints in migrations; let the database refuse impossible relationships.

commonMistakes.mistake: Editing schema by hand in a tool while migrations say otherwise.
commonMistakes.fix: Every schema change goes through a migration file - no exceptions, including 'quick experiments'.

agentGuidance: Make your agent draft the ER picture in text before coding: tables, columns, types, which columns reference which, and what cascades on delete. Approve the picture; the migration files then become mechanical transcription.

Migration runs cleanly twice: once on fresh database, once upgrading existing Level-1 data

Existing-data upgrade path preserves records while adding ownership
Orphan insert attempt fails with a database-level foreign key error
Join endpoint returns expense rows enriched with owner name correctly
architecture: All schema lives in versioned migrations; zero hand-edited schema state
Down-migration tested and restores pre-upgrade schema
security: Referential integrity enforced BY THE DATABASE, verified by direct attempt
testing: Both migration paths executed for real, outputs captured
Orphan-insert refusal demonstrated against the live database
production: README documents the schema diagram in text and the migrate/rollback commands

Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) migrations are versioned and include a tested rollback, (2) users and expenses relate through a real enforced foreign key, (3) an orphan insert genuinely fails at the database level, (4) the join endpoint returns owner-enriched rows correctly, (5) existing data survived the upgrade intact. Then try three creative corruptions - duplicate email, self-referencing nonsense, deleting a referenced user - and report which the database refused versus which slipped through.

What breaks first if foreign keys were removed but app code stayed the same?
Why must schema changes ship as migrations rather than manual edits?

title: Server-Side Validation and Errors
summary: Never trust the client, fail loudly inside, speak clearly outside - and log the whole story.
objective: Harden the API boundary: whitelist-validate everything arriving over HTTP, return uniform error envelopes, handle failures deliberately, and log enough to diagnose tomorrow's bug today.

vocabulary.meaning: The data carried inside a request or response body.
Accepting only known-good values and shapes, rejecting everything else by default.
One consistent JSON shape every error response uses.
Severity tag on a log line - info, warn, error - enabling filtering later.
The chain of function calls leading to an error - gold for diagnosis.

concepts.name: The client is an adversary's playground
concepts.explanation: Anything delivered to the browser can be modified, replayed or skipped entirely. curl needs no form and respects no rules. Server-side checks are not redundancy - they are the only checks that exist.

concepts.name: Fail loud inside, speak calm outside
concepts.explanation: Internally, errors deserve full stack traces and noisy logs. Externally, clients get disciplined envelopes: what happened, in their vocabulary, minus internal details like file paths and queries. Leaked internals are reconnaissance gifts.

explanations.title: Bypassing the browser in ten seconds
explanations.body: Open a terminal, POST invalid JSON straight at the API. Whatever frontend validation existed is now irrelevant. This single exercise - doing it deliberately - permanently installs the never-trust-client reflex.

explanations.title: Logs are tomorrow's memory
explanations.body: Three weeks from now, someone will ask why orders failed at 3am. The answer will exist only if today's code logged request identity, action and outcome - WITHOUT passwords, tokens or personal payloads. Logging secrets converts your log file into a liability.

examples.title: The uniform envelope
examples.description: Every failure answers { "error": { "code": "VALIDATION", "message": "amount must be positive" } }. Clients learn ONE parsing rule for ALL failures. Consistency here is API kindness.

examples.title: Good line versus bad line
examples.description: Good: WARN POST /expenses 400 ip=1.2.3.4 reason=amount_negative. Bad: logging the full payload including someone's password field. Same event; one is diagnosable, the other is a breach.

commonMistakes.mistake: Empty catch blocks swallowing errors into silence.
commonMistakes.fix: Every caught error gets logged with context and produces a deliberate response - silence is never acceptable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Validating only the happy shape (present and non-empty) while ignoring type absurdities.

title: Authentication
summary: Proving who someone is - hashed passwords, sessions and the habits that keep accounts safe.
objective: Implement real login: register and authenticate users with properly hashed passwords, maintain sessions via secure cookies, protect routes, and avoid the classic credential-storage mistakes.

vocabulary.meaning: Verifying WHO someone is - the login half of security.
A one-way scramble of a password; the original cannot be recovered from it.
Random data mixed into hashing so identical passwords produce different hashes.
Server memory of a logged-in user, referenced by a cookie the browser presents.
A cookie JavaScript cannot read - stolen only via far harder attack classes.

concepts.name: Hash, never encrypt, never store
concepts.explanation: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashes are not reversible at all. Passwords get hashed WITH a salt using a purpose-built slow algorithm. If you can ever show a user their password back, the design is already broken.

concepts.name: Sessions turn login into memory
concepts.explanation: Passwords travel once, at login. The session cookie then says 'this is user 7' on every later request. The server keeps the mapping; the cookie carries only an opaque id - httpOnly so page scripts cannot steal it.

explanations.title: Generic errors are a feature
explanations.body: 'Invalid email or password' for BOTH wrong-email and wrong-password cases. The moment your app reveals 'no such email', attackers gain a free list of registered accounts - half the work of breaking in, donated by you.

explanations.title: Login endpoints get special suspicion
explanations.body: Login is the internet's front door and favorite target: credential-stuffing replays stolen passwords millions of times. Even a simple rate limit - five attempts per minute per account - turns industrial attacks into impractical ones.

examples.title: Same password, different hashes
examples.description: Register two accounts with password123 and inspect the database: two completely different stored values. That is salted hashing proving itself - a leaked hash reveals nothing about sibling accounts.

examples.title: The protected route reflex
examples.description: Anonymous request to /expenses gets 401 with the error envelope. Every protected route asks the session 'who is this?' before anything else - uniformly, via one middleware, not scattered ifs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling custom crypto or 'just encoding' passwords (base64 is NOT security).
commonMistakes.fix: Use a standard, boring, well-tested hashing library. Cryptographic creativity is how breaches happen.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting a userId sent in the request body or URL.
commonMistakes.fix: Identity comes from the VERIFIED session server-side, nowhere else. Anything else is a costume party invitation.

agentGuidance: Before any auth code, require your agent to answer in writing: which hashing library and parameters, where sessions live, what the cookie flags are, and what the generic error message is. Four answers reviewed up front prevent four breach classes later.

title: Authorization and Roles
summary: Who may do what - ownership checks, roles and the least-privilege mindset.
objective: Enforce per-user data isolation and role-based permissions server-side, centralize authorization decisions, and internalize that hiding buttons is not access control.

vocabulary.meaning: Deciding WHAT an authenticated identity may do - the other half of security.
Confirming a record belongs to the requester before operating on it.
A named bundle of permissions - admin, member - assigned to users.
Insecure Direct Object Reference: reaching others' records by guessing URLs or ids.
Granting the minimum permissions needed - nothing extra 'for later'.

concepts.name: Authentication is not authorization
concepts.explanation: Logging in proves identity; it grants NOTHING by itself. Every operation re-asks: may THIS user act on THAT record? The question is asked fresh on every request, forever, no exceptions.

concepts.name: Guards are code, not CSS
concepts.explanation: Hidden menu items and disabled buttons are decoration. The API is the castle: if DELETE /expenses/43 lacks an ownership check, anyone logged-in deletes anyone's data by typing the URL. Authorization lives where the data lives.

explanations.title: IDOR: the one-change exploit
explanations.body: Authenticated user changes /expenses/41 to /expenses/42 and reads a stranger's data. No hacking tools - one edited digit. Prevention: every fetch/update/delete query includes WHERE user_id = current_session_user. Ownership rides along with every query, automatically.

explanations.title: Deny by default
explanations.body: New routes start forbidden until explicitly permitted. The reverse - open until someone remembers to restrict - guarantees eventual leaks. Whitelist thinking applies to permissions exactly as it did to input.

examples.title: Two roles, visible difference
examples.description: Owner role manages workspace members; member role sees tasks. The permission matrix is three lines long - and every line maps to one guard function. Small matrices stay auditable; sprawling ones rot.

examples.title: Centralized guard in action
examples.description: requireOwnership('expense') runs before update/delete handlers. One function, one place to audit, applied everywhere via route wiring. Scattered if-checks across twenty handlers WILL miss one eventually.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the target record first, checking ownership second - or trusting an id from the request body.
commonMistakes.fix: Identity comes from the session; scope every query by it. Fetch-with-filter beats fetch-then-hope.

commonMistakes.mistake: Granting broad permissions 'temporarily' during development.
commonMistakes.fix: Develop with the real permission matrix from day one; temporary openings become permanent breaches.

agentGuidance: Have your agent emit the full permission matrix as a table - role x action x allowed - before implementation, then wire every route through named guard functions matching that matrix. The matrix becomes your audit artifact and your test checklist simultaneously.

title: Testing Your App
summary: Executable proof that your app behaves - unit tests, integration tests and calm failure reading.
objective: Build an automated safety net around critical behavior, direct agents to write meaningful tests, review them skeptically, and treat a red suite as the emergency it is.

vocabulary.meaning: Checks one small piece of logic in isolation - a function with known inputs and outputs.
Checks pieces working TOGETHER - a request traveling through auth, guards and store.
The statement inside a test that must be true - the actual check.
Reusable known test data so tests start from predictable states.
A test that passes and fails without code changes - trust erosion incarnate.

concepts.name: Tests are executable DoD
concepts.explanation: Your Definition of Done lists behaviors; tests PROVE them on every run. Manual verification decays and gets skipped; suites execute identically forever. The best DoD items convert into test names almost word for word.

concepts.name: Meaningful beats exhaustive
concepts.explanation: Ten tests covering money math edge cases, permission denials and the auth journey outweigh two hundred trivial assertions. Test what BREAKS matters: totals rounding wrong, guards leaking, sessions surviving logout.

explanations.title: Arrange, act, assert
explanations.body: Every test reads the same: ARRANGE known state (seeded user, two expenses), ACT once (call the function or endpoint), ASSERT the outcome (total equals X). Deviation from this rhythm is usually a test trying to do too much.

explanations.title: The mutation experiment
explanations.body: Want to know if tests actually bite? Break the code ON PURPOSE - flip a comparison sign - and rerun. Suite stays green? Your tests decorate, they do not defend. Fix the tests, revert the sabotage, keep the lesson.

examples.title: A unit test worth keeping
examples.description: calculateTotal([100.10, 200.20, 300.30]) asserts exactly 600.60 - catching float-rounding bugs that manual testing routinely misses. Money math is unit-test heaven: tiny, pure, catastrophic when wrong.

examples.title: An integration test worth keeping
examples.description: Register, login as user A, attempt to delete user B's expense, assert 403 AND that B's expense still exists. One test, three layers, the exact promise of Level 2 proven executable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chasing coverage percentages with hollow tests that assert nothing meaningful.
commonMistakes.fix: Cover critical BEHAVIORS; ignore the percentage. Coverage reports measure execution, not protection.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving failing tests red while continuing development.
commonMistakes.fix: Red suite means STOP: fix or explicitly disable-with-issue. A red suite everyone ignores is worse than no suite.

agentGuidance: Flip the delegation: ask your agent to WRITE TESTS FIRST from your DoD list, watch them fail, THEN implement until green. Reviewing test names against the DoD is the fastest spec-review you will ever do - and gaps show up as missing tests, not missing features discovered in production.

title: Ship: Team Task Manager
summary: The Level 2 finale - specify, build, verify and deploy a real multi-user product with roles.
objective: Combine every Level 2 skill into one delivery: write the brief first, direct the full build of a multi-user task manager with roles and guarded APIs, keep the suite green, and deploy it publicly with demo accounts.

vocabulary.meaning: The brief document describing what to build before building - purpose, features, acceptance criteria, non-goals.
Cutting features to protect quality gates - deciding what NOT to build.
A quick post-deploy pass over critical flows proving the deployment breathes.
A throwaway seeded account letting outsiders try the app safely.

concepts.name: The brief comes first - always
concepts.explanation: You wrote a briefing document in Level 0; now it carries real weight. Features, acceptance criteria and non-goals agreed BEFORE code means every later argument is settled by pointing at the doc, not by renegotiating mid-build with an eager agent.

concepts.name: Quality gates outrank features
concepts.explanation: When schedule pressure meets quality gates, features lose. That ordering - suite green, guards audited, deploy verified - is what separates professional shipping from hope-driven deployment. A smaller shipped thing that works beats a bigger broken thing.

explanations.title: Composition is the exam
explanations.body: Nothing in this project is new: servers, schemas, validation, authN, authZ, tests, deploys - every ingredient exists in your earlier builds. What IS new is holding all of them in one coherent specification and verifying them as a system. That integration burden is the actual skill being certified.

explanations.title: Scope cuts are wins
explanations.body: Due dates, notifications and comments all sound vital until the suite is red and guards are unaudited. Cutting them - visibly, in writing, as scope decisions - IS the senior move this module teaches.

examples.title: A right-sized v1
examples.description: Workspaces with two roles; tasks with title, assignee and three statuses; membership managed by owners. Everything else - labels, search, activity feeds - explicitly listed as non-goals. That fits in days and ships solid.

examples.title: Demo accounts done right
examples.description: Seed demo-owner@ and demo-member@ accounts with obviously fake data and throwaway passwords, documented in the README. Outsiders explore freely; nothing real is at risk. Never seed real-looking personal data for demos.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the agent talk you into extra features mid-build.
commonMistakes.fix: New ideas go on a parking-lot list in the brief. v1 ships the agreed slice; the parking lot waits for v2.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deploying with the suite red because 'the feature works locally'.
commonMistakes.fix: Red suite equals no deploy. Fix, revert or cut - those are the only doors out.

agentGuidance: Structure the whole engagement as phases mirroring your skills: brief approval, schema and permission matrix approval, API skeleton, authN+authZ, test suite green, deploy rehearsal, production smoke. Demand a short completion report per phase against ITS exit criteria - you are running the loop you learned, at project scale.
